title: Go to a teacher, fuel in hand (1.2)
hook: the leaky boats can't cross, so the Mundaka says what to do next: go to a teacher, carrying firewood

segments.voice: Yesterday: plava, the rites as unsteady boats. Good for the lake, not for the ocean. Your line was the boat leaks.

When you show up at someone's house for the first time, you bring something. Flowers. A dish. Not because they need it. Because it says: I came on purpose, and I'm not just here to take. In ancient India, a student going to a teacher brought something too. Not money, not a gift for the shelf. Firewood: sticks for the teacher's sacred fire. The Mundaka has just said the rites can't carry you across. So what can? Its answer is a person, and a bundle of sticks.
screen: `YOU BRING SOMETHING TO THE DOOR.` → `NOT MONEY. FIREWOOD.` → `WHAT CAN CARRY YOU ACROSS?`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, Mundaka 1.2.12. Having looked closely at the worlds won by works, a seeker should come to dispassion. The uncreated isn't won by the made. To know that, let him go, fuel in hand, to a teacher who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman. Samitpanih: samit, firewood, the sticks for the sacred fire; pani, hand. Fuel in hand. You met this a few days ago, when the six students came to Pippalada samitpanayah, with fuel in their hands. It's the old sign of a real student. It says: I'll serve. I'll help keep your fire going. I'm ready to live the life, not just ask the question. And notice the two qualities named for the teacher. Shrotriya: learned in the Veda, someone who has heard and studied. And brahmanishtha: established in Brahman, someone who lives what they know. Both. Knowledge without living it isn't enough, and living without knowledge isn't either. Then the next verse gives the teacher a duty too. To a student who has come properly, whose mind is calm and settled, the wise teacher should teach, truly, the knowledge by which one knows the imperishable. So the student brings fuel. The teacher brings fire. Both owe something. In many Hindu traditions this relationship, guru and shishya, is still the heart of how the deepest teaching passes on, from teacher to student, voice to ear.
screen: `THE MADE CAN'T WIN THE UNMADE.` · `GO TO A TEACHER, FUEL IN HAND.` · `LEARNED, AND ESTABLISHED IN BRAHMAN.` · `THE TEACHER MUST TEACH, TRULY.` · then, large: `SAMITPANI.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that mattered: a parent, a coach, an elder, someone in a book, maybe someone who never knew they taught you. Picture them clearly, and ask what fuel you brought them, or could bring someone teaching you now: patience, attention, showing up. Let one of those be your bundle of sticks.

Brahmanishtha, established in Brahman, one mark of a true teacher. The Mundaka's instruction: go, fuel in hand, to one who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman, who then must teach truly.
Your line: samitpani. Tomorrow, the fire that fuel was for. Day four hundred fourteen, done.

howItsDone: In many Hindu traditions students approach a teacher with an offering and study in the guru-shishya relationship; Guru Purnima, on the full moon of Ashadha, is a day many set aside to honor their teachers.

chat.says: What does the Mundaka say to look for in a spiritual teacher?
options: Someone learned in the Veda who also lives it, established in Brahman.
Someone famous with many followers, whatever they actually know.
Someone who knows every book, even if they don't live it.
chat.meaning: The Mundaka names two marks of a teacher: shrotriya, learned in the Veda, and brahmanishtha, established in Brahman. Knowing and living, both.
